summary: An informational memo describing the procedures and criteria the IETF Transport Area uses to review reliable multicast protocols, because applications exist that need reliable delivery to many receivers at once.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo sets out how the IETF Transport Area would review reliable multicast proposals. It requires technical evidence that a proposal can scale, control congestion, and protect the network before publication.

questions: why is reliable multicast hard to standardize
subtitle: Review procedures and technical criteria for reliable multicast proposals in the IETF Transport Area.

tldr.problem: Applications need reliable delivery to multicast groups, but different applications need different reliability behavior and weak congestion control could damage the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines Transport Area review procedures and requires proposals to analyze scalability, congestion control, robustness, trials, containment, security, and privacy.
tldr.outcome: Drafts meeting the criteria default to Experimental RFC status; standards-track proposals face at least as stringent a review. The memo is Informational and specifies no protocol.

facts.label: Example group scale
facts.value: Thousands or tens of thousands of members

today: RFC 2357 is an Informational memo published in June 1998. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it defines review procedures, not a multicast protocol.

sections.title: Who Reviews Reliable Multicast Proposals
sections.content:
The Transport Area Directors (ADs) review reliable multicast Internet-Drafts, including drafts submitted by individuals rather than working groups. The memo describes criteria for considering such drafts for any RFC publication status.

For a Standards Track proposal, failure to meet the criteria means the ADs will not support publication. For Experimental or Informational proposals, the ADs may recommend publication with an IESG note saying that the protocol does not comply with the criteria. Drafts meeting the technical criteria default to Experimental status.
sections.plainLanguage: The Transport Area Directors review reliable multicast proposals before publication. A proposal that fails the criteria cannot proceed as a standard, and may be published with a note describing its failure.

sections.title: Why Reliable Multicast Needs Extra Care
sections.content:
Reliable multicast adds delivery guarantees to multicast, which otherwise offers best-effort group delivery without guarantees. Applications such as collaborative tools, distributed virtual reality, and software upgrades may need it.

The memo says one protocol is unlikely to meet all applications' needs. Applications differ in ordering, number of senders, group size, delay needs, bandwidth, and whether timely delivery matters more than complete reliability. The technical problem is also more complex than reliable unicast.
sections.plainLanguage: Different group applications need different kinds of delivery. A single reliable multicast design is unlikely to fit all of them.

sections.title: Congestion Risks
sections.content:
The memo's main concern is the effect of reliable multicast on other traffic during congestion, especially competing TCP traffic. The Internet depends on senders reducing traffic when a link is congested; the memo says TCP congestion control is what prevents congestion collapse in the Internet described there.

A single multicast flow can reach a large global tree. Human users may stop an unintelligible audio or video stream, but computer-to-computer file transfers can continue until delivery completes. Such transfers may last indefinitely and can generate large amounts of control traffic such as acknowledgements, negative acknowledgements, and status messages.

The review process is intended to encourage research while preventing widespread use of protocols with inadequate congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer may keep retrying a group transfer even when the network is overloaded. A reliable multicast protocol must reduce its traffic enough to protect other network users.

sections.title: Technical Review Criteria
sections.content:
A draft must analyze its behavior, including scalability, congestion control, error recovery, and robustness, and explain vulnerabilities and performance problems. It must describe trials or simulations that support the design. It must analyze whether congestion avoidance can cope with the global Internet and document conditions that could cause congestion harm and how to prevent it.

If the protocol could damage the Internet, the draft must discuss ways to limit its scope or contain it. It must analyze security and privacy for each secure mode, identify which participants must be trusted, consider whether receivers can detect different copies of data, and explain how retransmission abuse is controlled. The draft must also describe required and provided key management. A mechanism more aggressive than TCP faces a great burden of proof that it does not threaten network stability.
sections.plainLanguage: Proposals must explain how they behave at scale, how they respond to congestion, and what testing supports the design. They must also address containment, security, privacy, and key management.

sections.title: Publication Path
sections.content:
The ADs may recommend that a closely related individual draft be brought into the IETF, or that it be published as Experimental or Informational, possibly with an IESG annotation. Reliable multicast work may develop in the IRTF research group or in a focused IETF working group with an Experimental product.

When the technology matures enough for standardization, the Transport Area may charter working groups to develop Standards Track documents. Their criteria will be at least as stringent as those in this memo. The memo also says RFC 1301 and RFC 1458 were published before reliable-multicast congestion effects were fully appreciated and should be deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: Reliable multicast proposals begin as research or experiments. A later Standards Track proposal must pass review criteria at least as strict as this memo's.
